strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: integrating scene understanding, trajectory planning, and future visual prediction for autonomous driving world models. The goal is relevant to computer vision and embodied decision-making, and the framing around avoiding text-only bottlenecks is well motivated.

The proposed UniDrive-WM is evaluated on Bench2Drive with both closed-loop and open-loop metrics, plus future-frame generation metrics. Reporting Driving Score, Success Rate, L2 trajectory error, collision-related metrics, detection metrics, FID, and VQA metrics gives a reasonably broad empirical picture.

The results are promising relative to strong recent baselines such as ORION: closed-loop Driving Score improves from 77.74 to 79.22, Success Rate from 54.62 to 56.36, average L2 from 0.68 to 0.64, and perception metrics also improve. The ablation suggests that adding image generation improves planning and detection compared with the planner/perception-only variants.

The paper usefully compares two design choices for future image prediction, discrete autoregressive generation and AR+diffusion, and discusses their trade-offs in planning performance, resolution, and generation cost. This is a valuable direction for autonomous-driving world models.
The manuscript is generally understandable and includes architecture diagrams, equations, main results, ablations, and supplementary tables/visualizations.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental. Much of the architecture appears to build directly on ORION/QT-Former plus known unified understanding-generation ideas and known AR/diffusion image-generation mechanisms. The paper’s distinctive contribution is mainly the coupling and training recipe, but the manuscript does not sufficiently isolate which parts are new versus inherited.

The empirical gains over the closest baseline are modest in the most important closed-loop metrics: Driving Score improves by about 1.5 absolute points and Success Rate by about 1.7 points over ORION. These may be meaningful, but no variance, confidence intervals, repeated runs, or statistical analysis are provided, making it hard to judge robustness on the relatively small closed-loop evaluation protocol.

The ablation evidence does not fully substantiate the central causal claim that planning-conditioned image generation provides a strong world-model benefit. The ablation compares module combinations, but does not control for additional parameters, training compute, auxiliary supervision, VQA mixing, or alternative auxiliary losses. It is also unclear how much of the gain comes from future-image prediction itself versus extra representation learning.

The method description lacks important reproducibility details: loss weights, training schedules, data mixture ratios, prompt templates, exact tokenization/codebook details, image-token resolution handling, inference procedure, decoding settings, and runtime/latency are underspecified. For an autonomous driving method, compute and inference latency are especially important.

The image-generation evaluation is not fully convincing. FID alone is a weak proxy for driving-relevant future prediction, and comparisons to prior generation methods may be affected by different resolutions, protocols, conditioning information, and generated horizons. The paper would be stronger with trajectory-consistency metrics, object-level future-state accuracy, temporal consistency, or human/simulator-based evaluations.

There are internal inconsistencies in the discussion of AR versus AR+diffusion. The text suggests AR+diffusion can yield superior visual quality, but the reported FID is worse than AR, and planning metrics are also slightly worse. The claim that the diffusion branch is trained with deterministic reconstruction while using a diffusion/flow-matching formulation is also confusing and needs clearer explanation.

The evaluation is limited to Bench2Drive/CARLA. Given the claim of a unified autonomous-driving world model, evidence on additional datasets, real-world driving benchmarks, or cross-scenario generalization would be important. The paper does not convincingly show robustness to distribution shift, long-horizon interaction, or safety-critical rare events.

The manuscript contains several clarity and polish issues, including repeated references, grammar errors, formatting issues in tables, and an incomplete project-page sentence in the abstract. These do not invalidate the work, but they reduce confidence in the maturity of the submission.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: coupling perception, future prediction, and trajectory planning for autonomous driving within a VLM-centric world-model framework.
The idea of using trajectory-conditioned future image prediction as an auxiliary signal for planning is plausible, and the paper explores both discrete autoregressive and AR+diffusion variants.

The experiments report improvements over ORION on Bench2Drive, including DS 77.74 to 79.22, SR 54.62 to 56.36, and modest gains in open-loop L2/collision metrics. The ablation suggests image generation may help relative to a no-image-generation variant.
The paper includes several relevant metrics across planning, detection, image generation, and VQA rather than evaluating only one output modality.
weaknesses: The scientific contribution appears incremental over ORION and existing driving world-model / VLM-planning work. Much of the system is inherited from ORION, QT-Former, Vicuna, EVA-02, MoVQGAN/diffusion components, and standard auxiliary losses; the paper does not clearly isolate a novel algorithmic mechanism beyond adding future-image generation heads.

The empirical gains are small and not supported by statistical analysis. The main closed-loop improvement over ORION is about 1.5 DS and 1.7 SR points, and open-loop L2 improves from 0.68 to 0.64. No variance, repeated runs, route-level significance, or robustness analysis is provided, which is concerning for CARLA/Bench2Drive evaluations.

The evidence for the central claim that future image generation improves planning is incomplete. The ablation is mainly open-loop and does not convincingly rule out confounders such as extra supervision, extra training stages, different parameter counts, or mixed VQA/driving training. Closed-loop ablations of the image-generation module are missing.

The method is under-specified in important places. The trajectory planner introduces a Gaussian latent variable but omits KL regularization and gives little detail on sampling/inference, latent dimensionality, or distribution learning. The AR+diffusion description is also confusing: it uses flow matching but then says inference is deterministic reconstruction, making the generative interpretation unclear.

The image-generation evaluation is not rigorous enough. FID comparisons against prior world models may be affected by different image resolutions, input modalities, horizons, splits, or evaluation protocols, but these are not controlled or discussed. Qualitative figures are sparse and do not demonstrate safety-relevant causal consistency.

The paper repeatedly claims bidirectional information and gradient flow between reasoning, action, and generation, but the architecture and experiments do not substantiate this beyond joint losses. There is no analysis showing that generated futures are actually used by the planner at inference or that gradients from image prediction improve specific planning behaviors.

The benchmark scope is narrow: all main results are on Bench2Drive/CARLA, with only 950 training scenes and 50 open-loop validation scenes. There is no real-world dataset evaluation, cross-town/weather generalization, long-horizon evaluation, or safety stress testing, despite strong claims about autonomous driving world models.

Some reported improvements are marginal for the added system complexity. The VQA gains are tiny, e.g. CIDEr 65.7 to 66.3, BLEU 52.4 to 52.9, ROUGE-L 77.5 to 78.3, and the AR+diffusion branch is worse than AR on planning despite being presented as a major design path.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says a project page is available but leaves it blank; implementation details, hyperparameters, compute cost, training schedules, inference latency, and exact evaluation settings are insufficient for reproducing the claims.

The paper has substantial clarity and polish issues, including grammatical errors, vague formulations, inconsistent terminology, and over-claiming. There is also little meaningful limitations or societal-impact discussion for an autonomous-driving system, where failure modes and safety assumptions are central.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: integrating scene understanding, trajectory planning, and future visual prediction for autonomous driving world models. The contribution type is best viewed as Algorithms/General, and the evaluation is appropriately centered on planning and generation performance rather than only proposing a standalone image generator.

The proposed UniDrive-WM framework is conceptually appealing. Coupling VLM reasoning, a differentiable trajectory planner, and trajectory-conditioned future-frame generation is a meaningful direction, and the comparison between discrete AR generation and AR+diffusion continuous generation adds useful design insight.

The empirical results are strong on Bench2Drive. The method improves over a strong ORION baseline in closed-loop driving score and success rate, and also improves open-loop L2 error, collision metrics, detection metrics, and FID for future-frame generation.

The ablation study supports the central claim that future image generation provides useful auxiliary supervision for planning: removing image generation degrades trajectory accuracy and collision-related metrics, while combining detection, planning, and image generation gives the best reported results.

The paper evaluates multiple aspects of the system, including closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, detection, future image generation, VQA, and multi-ability driving categories. This breadth makes the experimental case more convincing than a single-metric benchmark result.
weaknesses: The novelty is partly incremental because the system builds heavily on ORION/QT-Former and combines several existing ideas: VLM-based planning, auxiliary perception heads, autoregressive visual tokens, and diffusion-style reconstruction. The architectural integration is useful, but the paper could more clearly isolate what is fundamentally new versus inherited from prior systems.

The evidence is concentrated on Bench2Drive/CARLA. Since autonomous driving world models are highly sensitive to simulator bias, weather/domain shifts, and long-tail interactions, the lack of real-world validation or cross-dataset generalization limits confidence in broader impact.

The image-generation evaluation is relatively thin. FID and qualitative frames do not fully establish whether generated futures are causally useful, geometrically accurate, temporally consistent, or safety-relevant. Metrics for trajectory-image alignment, dynamic-object consistency, or multi-step rollout fidelity would strengthen the case.

Some claims about AR+diffusion are not fully aligned with the reported numbers. The text suggests superior visual quality or high-resolution potential for AR+diffusion, but the reported FID is worse than the AR branch, and the main training details mention 256x256 rather than the 512x512 potential discussed later.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a large system trained on 8 H200 GPUs. The paper gives high-level hyperparameters but lacks enough information about optimization schedules, loss weights, sampling/inference cost, tokenization details, and release status to make independent reproduction straightforward.

The closed-loop improvements over ORION are positive but modest in some key metrics, and there is no statistical analysis over route variance or multiple seeds. For a safety-critical setting, confidence intervals or repeated evaluations would make the reported gains more persuasive.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: coupling VLM-based driving reasoning, trajectory planning, and future visual prediction in a unified autonomous-driving world-model framework.

The experimental scope is broad, covering Bench2Drive closed-loop/open-loop planning, nuScenes open-loop planning, future-frame FID, detection metrics, and VQA metrics. The reported results are consistently competitive, with improvements over the ORION backbone on Bench2Drive planning and perception metrics.

The comparison between discrete AR generation and AR+Diffusion is useful. The paper gives a reasonable discussion of the speed/quality trade-off and reports both planning and image-generation outcomes for the two variants.

Ablations support the main empirical claim that adding future image prediction and ordering planning before generation improves planning accuracy, collision metrics, and FID, even if the gains are moderate.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to ORION and recent unified understanding/generation models. Much of the perception backbone, planning formulation, and training recipe are inherited; the main new component appears to be adding planning-conditioned future-image generation rather than a fundamentally new world-model mechanism.

The central claim of bidirectional coupling between reasoning, action, and generation is not fully substantiated. Since planning tokens are generated before image tokens, future-image generation cannot refine the trajectory at inference time; the planning gains seem to come mainly from auxiliary training supervision rather than an interactive or closed-loop world-model rollout.

Several improvements are modest. On Bench2Drive closed-loop, the gain over ORION is about 1.5 DS points and 1.8 SR points; on nuScenes, collision rate is worse than FSDrive despite better L2. This makes the practical impact less decisive than the paper’s wording suggests.

The AR+Diffusion branch has poor runtime feasibility for driving deployment: 0.4 fps on A100. Yet it is included in planning comparisons without a clear account of how this affects closed-loop evaluation or real-time use.

The future-world modeling evidence is limited mostly to single future front-view frame prediction and FID. There is little evaluation of long-horizon consistency, multi-view consistency, controllability under alternative actions, causal counterfactuals, or whether generated futures are physically/geometrically faithful beyond visual quality metrics.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The project-page sentence appears to omit the actual URL, and important implementation details such as exact training schedules, loss weights, data mixing ratios, and baseline reimplementation/fairness protocols are not sufficiently specified in the extracted manuscript.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: integrating VLM-based reasoning, trajectory planning, and future-frame prediction for autonomous driving world models.
The experimental section covers several relevant tasks and benchmarks, including Bench2Drive closed-loop/open-loop metrics, nuScenes planning, future-frame FID, VQA, and some ablations.
The comparison between discrete AR generation and AR+Diffusion is a useful design axis, and the paper reports practical trade-offs in fidelity and inference speed.
The reported numbers are generally favorable relative to ORION and other baselines, especially in open-loop planning and future-frame FID.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited and not convincingly separated from ORION plus an added future-image generation head. Much of the architecture, perception backbone, trajectory planner, and training setup are inherited, while the proposed coupling is only weakly specified.

Several central claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly claims bidirectional coupling, gradient flow between reasoning/action/generation, and iterative refinement of trajectory generation, but the method mainly adds auxiliary image-generation losses conditioned on predicted/planning tokens. It is unclear that generated futures are used to refine planning at inference or that there is a true world-model rollout mechanism.

The method description lacks key implementation details needed for reproducibility: optimizer and schedules, loss weights, exact image horizon, trajectory horizon, data mixing ratios, prompts/VQA formatting, codebook/MoVQGAN setup, diffusion decoder architecture, sampling/reconstruction procedure, and training cost beyond GPU type.

The empirical gains do not fully support the broad claims. Closed-loop improvement over ORION is small, while the strongest claimed percentage gains appear to rely on selected open-loop metrics. No variance, confidence intervals, or repeated closed-loop runs are reported, which is important for Bench2Drive-style evaluation.

The ablations are too shallow to establish causality. The paper does not adequately isolate whether improvements come from future-frame supervision, extra parameters/training, different resolution/decoder capacity, longer training, or VQA mixed training. There is no strong control with a matched auxiliary loss or matched compute.

The image-generation evaluation is weak for a world-model claim. FID and qualitative examples are insufficient for assessing temporal consistency, controllability by trajectory, multi-view consistency, safety-relevant object dynamics, or whether generated images improve downstream planning beyond generic auxiliary supervision.

There are concerns about fair comparison and attribution. Some baselines may use different modalities, conditions, datasets, or evaluation protocols; the paper acknowledges metric differences for some methods but does not fully normalize comparisons. The future-frame baselines are also not clearly trained/evaluated under identical conditioning.

The planning/safety evidence is incomplete. Collision and boundary losses rely on predicted perception outputs, but the paper does not analyze failure cases, safety-critical scenarios, long-horizon robustness, distribution shift, or whether hallucinated future frames can degrade decisions.

The VQA evidence is not very convincing. The reported gains are small, metrics are mostly surface-form generation metrics or ChatGPT scoring, and qualitative examples include potentially inconsistent driving advice, such as describing a red light while also saying to keep speed/lane follow.

Presentation quality is uneven. The project-page sentence is blank, several tables are crowded or hard to read, there are typographical/formatting issues, and some claims in the abstract/introduction are stronger than what the experiments demonstrate.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: unifying VLM-based scene understanding, trajectory planning, and future visual prediction for autonomous driving. The contribution type is not explicitly declared, so I assess it as Algorithms/General; under that framing, the integration of planning-conditioned future generation with VLM reasoning is a meaningful systems/algorithmic contribution.

The empirical case is strong overall. UniDrive-WM improves over ORION and other end-to-end driving baselines on Bench2Drive closed-loop driving score and success rate, improves open-loop L2 and collision metrics on Bench2Drive, and shows competitive nuScenes planning results. The gains are consistent rather than isolated.

The paper evaluates multiple facets of the proposed model: planning, 3D detection/perception metrics, future-frame FID, VQA, closed-loop multi-ability results, and ablations. This breadth supports the central claim that future visual prediction can provide useful auxiliary supervision for planning and reasoning.

The comparison between discrete AR and AR+Diffusion generation is useful. The paper clearly identifies a practical trade-off between the faster AR branch and the higher-fidelity but much slower AR+Diffusion branch, which is valuable for autonomous-driving deployment considerations.

The ablations are well aligned with the method’s claims: removing image generation degrades planning and collision metrics, changing the ordering of planning and generation worsens both planning and FID, and adding image generation modestly improves VQA metrics. These experiments make the proposed coupling more convincing.
weaknesses: The novelty is partly incremental because the system builds heavily on ORION/QT-Former, uses standard LoRA/Vicuna/EVA components, and combines known AR and diffusion generation paradigms. The paper’s main contribution is integration and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new planning or generation mechanism.

Some technical details are under-specified for full reproducibility. The abstract says the project page is available but no URL is shown in the extracted manuscript, and the training recipe lacks several important details such as learning rates, batch sizes, schedules, loss weights, data mixing ratios, and exact image-tokenization settings.

The causal interpretation that future image generation improves planning is plausible but not fully isolated. The image-generation branch adds auxiliary supervision and capacity, so it is hard to distinguish whether gains come from genuine world-modeling/visual imagination, regularization, additional training signal, or increased model size/compute.

The image-generation evaluation is relatively narrow. FID on future front-view frames is useful but insufficient for driving relevance; the paper would be stronger with trajectory-conditioned consistency metrics, object/agent motion accuracy, temporal consistency, and safety-critical scenario breakdowns.

Several claims about bidirectional information flow and gradient flow are stronger than the evidence shown. The architecture conditions image generation on planning tokens, but the paper does not deeply analyze whether generated future frames are actually used at inference to refine planning, or whether the benefit is primarily from joint training.

The AR+Diffusion branch is too slow for practical closed-loop deployment as reported, at 0.4 fps on an A100, and the paper leaves speedup as future work. This does not undermine the scientific contribution, but it limits the immediate applied impact of the highest-fidelity variant.

The paper would benefit from a more explicit limitations and safety discussion, especially given the autonomous-driving domain. Failure modes under rare events, distribution shift, hallucinated future frames, and reliance on synthetic Bench2Drive closed-loop evaluation deserve more careful treatment.
